nameStory: Marsh valerian gets its name from its love of wetlands - 'marsh' referring to its soggy habitat preferences, while 'valerian' comes from the Latin 'valere' meaning 'to be strong,' likely referring to the plant's potent medicinal properties. The species name 'uliginosa' literally means 'of swampy places,' doubling down on this plant's commitment to wet feet!
description: Marsh valerian is a delicate perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall in New England's wetlands. It produces clusters of tiny, fragrant white or pale pink flowers that bloom in early summer, creating a soft, cloud-like appearance above the foliage. The plant has distinctive compound leaves that are divided into narrow leaflets, giving it a feathery texture. Despite being in the honeysuckle family, it looks quite different from the woody honeysuckle vines most people know.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink flowers arranged in dense, rounded clusters at stem tips, each flower only about 1/8 inch across with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's strongest in the evening

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 3-7 narrow, toothed leaflets that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in small colonies from creeping underground stems, with multiple upright stems rising 1-3 feet tall from the wetland soil

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny dry fruits with feathery white plumes that help them float on water and catch the wind, appearing in late summer

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, hollow stems that are often reddish at the base and feel somewhat succulent when gently squeezed

habitat: Marsh valerian thrives in calcareous wetlands, meaning lime-rich marshes, fens, and wet meadows throughout New England. Look for it along the edges of streams, in boggy areas with alkaline soils, and in wet prairies where it often grows alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. It's particularly fond of areas that stay consistently moist but aren't permanently flooded.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish shoots in late spring, with the characteristic compound leaves unfurling in a feathery pattern.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer, when the sweet-scented flower clusters are most prominent and attractive to small butterflies and beneficial insects.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to fluffy seed heads that persist into autumn, while leaves may turn yellow-green before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground stems, leaving no above-ground traces until spring returns.

funFact: Marsh valerian's flowers are actually most fragrant at dusk and during the night - this nocturnal perfume is designed to attract moths as pollinators, making evening the best time to experience this plant's sweet, honey-like scent that can carry surprisingly far on still air!
confusionNotes: With only 9 recorded observations in New England, marsh valerian is easily confused with its more common cousin, garden valerian, but marsh valerian is much smaller and always found in wetlands rather than disturbed upland areas. Remember: 'marsh' means wet feet - if you're not in soggy soil, you're probably looking at a different valerian.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'valerian,' this plant is now classified in the honeysuckle family rather than the traditional valerian family - a recent change that reflects new understanding of plant relationships through genetic studies. This reclassification can confuse field guides of different ages.
compareHints: Marsh valerian differs from common valerian by being much smaller (1-3 feet vs 3-6 feet), preferring wetlands over disturbed uplands, and having more delicate, feathery foliage. The flower clusters are also smaller and more rounded compared to common valerian's larger, more elongated flower heads, and marsh valerian's evening fragrance is distinctly sweeter and more honey-like.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common valerian is much taller and more robust than its relative marsh valerian, which stays under 2 feet tall and prefers wetter, more acidic soils.
